interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through the booking API you built for your capstone. How did your conflict-checking logic decide that two reservations overlap?
interviewQuestions.why: Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand the work you say you did and can explain your choices.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Use real details from your capstone: what the API did, how you handled overlapping bookings, and what you would change. Say clearly that it was a team capstone and which parts you built.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a list and a hash map, and when would you choose each?
interviewQuestions.why: This checks basic data structure knowledge that entry-level software roles often expect.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Explain it in plain words and connect it to your sorting visualizer or another project where you worked with data. If you are unsure about part of it, say so honestly.

interviewQuestions.question: How did you test your booking API, and how would you decide what else to test?
interviewQuestions.why: Testing habits matter for software and QA roles, and your pytest suite is some of your strongest evidence.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Describe what your pytest unit tests covered, including any edge cases you remember. Do not claim coverage numbers unless you know them.

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time something broke or a teammate disagreed during your capstone. What did you do?
interviewQuestions.why: Interviewers want to see how you handle problems and work with others.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Tell a short true story in four parts: the situation, your responsibility, what you did, and what happened. Use only events that really occurred.

interviewQuestions.question: This role mentions Docker and AWS as nice to have. What is your experience with them, and what questions do you have for us about the team?
interviewQuestions.why: Interviewers want an honest answer about a gap, and the questions you ask show what you care about.
interviewQuestions.whatGoodLooksLike: Say honestly that you have not used them yet, name what you are doing to learn Docker, and ask one or two real questions about onboarding, code review or how the team tests its work.

actions: Read the posting yourself. Note that it contains a strange hidden note aimed at AI tools, so treat it with caution and look for the employer's real careers page yourself. Done when you have a short note on whether it seems legitimate.
Confirm your degree status and graduation date. Done when you know what to write on the resume.
Read the resume draft and check each bullet against your own memory and the evidence ids. Fix anything that is not exactly true. Done when every bullet is something you could explain.
Do a free beginner Docker tutorial from the official Docker documentation for about two hours. Done when you can say in two sentences what a container is.

Try to run your capstone or a small Flask app in a Docker container on your own computer, if your setup allows. Done when you have either a working container or notes on where you got stuck. Do not add Docker to your resume unless you actually did it.
Practise the five interview questions out loud, using your own project details. Done when you have rough notes for each answer.
Remove any private data from your project code before putting it on a public portfolio, such as passwords or personal details.
Find two or three other entry-level software or QA postings, read them yourself and note what they ask for. Done when you have a short list of common requirements and any new gaps.
Review day: read your final resume and approve or change it yourself. Done when you have a version you are happy with.
Decide for yourself which postings to apply to and apply yourself using your own accounts. I cannot apply, email or contact anyone for you, and nobody can promise an interview or a job.
